title: Amazon RDS
notes: Research input only: FREQUENCY.md section 3 pairs (Multi-AZ vs read replica, RDS vs Aurora, RDS vs DynamoDB, RDS Proxy) and FRESHNESS.md RDS rows are hypotheses; every value must come from a saved AWS page.

demand.question: RDS Extended Support: what it is, that enrollment is automatic at the end of standard support, how long it lasts (hypothesis: up to three years), that it is billed per vCPU-hour, and how to opt out. Changed recently: charges from 2024-03-01.
Major versus minor engine versions: what auto minor version upgrade does, that major version upgrades are started by you, and what the maintenance window controls.

DB instance class types: general purpose (db.m), memory optimized (db.r, db.x, db.z), burstable (db.t). Which one for a memory-bound database, which for dev and test, and why burstable classes are not for steady production load?
demand.note: adjudicate-26: rds-class-t2-dev-test-only rejected (db.t2 is past end of support; the dev/test sentence applies only to db.t2). No verified fact says burstable classes are for dev/test only; teach the burstable baseline and Unlimited charge instead.

demand.question: Vertical scaling: can the instance class be changed on a running instance, is there downtime, and how does Multi-AZ reduce it (the standby is modified first, then failover)? What does 'apply immediately' versus the maintenance window mean?
Storage types and their ranges: gp2, gp3 (recommended), io1 (previous generation), io2 Block Express (recommended), magnetic. Minimum and maximum size and IOPS per engine from the storage tables.
gp3: the baseline IOPS and throughput included in the price, the storage size above which extra IOPS and throughput can be provisioned, and the maximum IOPS.
io2 Block Express: maximum IOPS (hypothesis 256,000), maximum throughput, durability claim, and the IOPS-to-storage ratio rule that also applies to storage autoscaling.
demand.note: numbers: io2 durability: not stated on CHAP_Storage or any saved RDS page (searched corpus for 99.999 and durability); belongs to the EBS chapter. Source contradiction recorded: io2 table says 16,000 MiB/s max throughput, comparison table says up to 4,000 MB/s.

demand.question: Maximum storage per DB instance: 64 TiB for most engines; 256 TiB for Oracle and SQL Server with additional storage volumes (changed 2025-11-14). Which engines stay at 64 TiB?
demand.note: adjudicate-26: rds-storage-sqlserver-max-16-tib rejected (stale sentence; the same page now gives up to 256 TiB for SQL Server with additional storage volumes).

demand.question: Magnetic storage is deprecated: restoring a snapshot to magnetic storage is not possible from 2026-07-01. What does the guide say, and what should a reader answer when an older question offers 'standard' storage?

Storage modifications: storage can only grow, never shrink; a manual increase must be at least 10 percent; how many storage modifications are allowed in 24 hours (changed 2026-07-15: up to four; before: once per six hours)?

Storage autoscaling: the three conditions that trigger an automatic increase (free space below 10 percent of allocated storage, the low-storage condition lasts at least five minutes, at least six hours since the last modification), the 'maximum storage threshold', and that the increase causes no downtime.

Storage autoscaling: what it does not do (never decreases storage, does not add IOPS for an IOPS-bound workload, does not apply to some engines or storage types?), and the stem signals ('unpredictable data growth', 'running out of space', 'minimal operational overhead').

Provisioned IOPS: when to choose io2 or io1 over gp3 (I/O-intensive, latency-sensitive OLTP, consistent performance), and when gp3 is enough. What does 'Provisioned IOPS' in the exam guide bullet refer to?
RDS Optimized Writes (MySQL, MariaDB) and RDS Optimized Reads (MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL): what each one does in one sentence and which instance classes they need.

Account quotas that questions use: DB instances per Region (hypothesis 40), read replicas per source (15), manual snapshots per Region (100), proxies per account, DB subnet groups, parameter groups. Take the rows from the quotas table with the header.
Constraints in the quotas page: DB instance identifier rules, master user name rules, storage ranges per engine (the constraints section).

Key CloudWatch metrics for capacity decisions: CPUUtilization, FreeableMemory, FreeStorageSpace, DatabaseConnections, ReadIOPS and WriteIOPS, BurstBalance, ReplicaLag. Which metric answers which stem?
demand.note: behavior: Per-metric definitions (FreeableMemory, FreeStorageSpace, DatabaseConnections, BurstBalance) are in rds-metrics page, not fetched by this lens.

demand.question: Multi-AZ DB instance deployment: one primary and one standby in a different Availability Zone, synchronous replication, the standby serves no read or write traffic, one DNS endpoint.
What makes Amazon RDS fail over automatically (Availability Zone outage, primary instance failure, instance class change, OS patching, host failure, manual reboot with failover)?
Failover time of a Multi-AZ DB instance: typically 60 to 120 seconds (the FAQ says one to two minutes). What can make it longer (large transactions, long recovery)?

What happens to the endpoint at failover: the CNAME is flipped to the standby, the application must reconnect, and DNS caching (for example a JVM TTL) can delay the reconnect. Why the application needs retry logic.

Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment: one writer and two readable standby DB instances in three Availability Zones, semisynchronous replication, separate writer and reader endpoints. Which engines support it (MySQL, PostgreSQL)?
Failover time of a Multi-AZ DB cluster: typically under 35 seconds. Minor version upgrade downtime of a Multi-AZ DB cluster: typically 35 seconds, one second or less with RDS Proxy.
Limitations of Multi-AZ DB clusters (engines and versions, instance classes, storage types gp3 and io1 and io2, no cross-Region read replica from a cluster?, Oracle and SQL Server not supported).
demand.note: behavior: Cross-Region read replica from a Multi-AZ DB cluster: not stated on the Limitations, cluster-concepts or MultiAZDBCluster_ReadRepl pages. Other limitation items (IPv6, Kerberos, option groups, stop/start, encrypting unencrypted cluster) are list lines too short to quote; fact rds-multi-az-cluster-no-cross-region-backups was rejected for that reason.

demand.question: Multi-AZ DB instance versus Multi-AZ DB cluster: standbys readable or not, replication mode, failover time, cost, engines. A compare table for 'Choose it or not'.
Converting a Single-AZ DB instance to Multi-AZ: done by modifying the instance, how RDS builds the standby (snapshot and restore), and the performance impact during conversion.

Backups and Multi-AZ: for a Multi-AZ DB instance the automated backup is taken from the standby, so the primary sees no I/O suspension (except for SQL Server?). For Single-AZ, a brief I/O suspension happens during the backup window.
Maintenance with Multi-AZ: OS updates are applied to the standby first, then a failover, then the old primary; what this means for downtime during patching.

Multi-AZ is inside one Region only. What does the guide say about Regions and Availability Zones for RDS, and which features cross Regions (cross-Region read replicas, cross-Region automated backups, snapshot copy)?
Manual forced failover (reboot with failover) to test the application's behavior, and the RDS events that announce a failover (event notification, EventBridge).

Hypothesis (FRESHNESS, What's New 2026-05-26): Amazon RDS supports ENA Express for Multi-AZ replication. What does the guide page say it changes (replication latency, bandwidth), on which instance classes? GA before 2026-07-15, so examinable but low priority.
Well-Architected reliability: deploy the workload to multiple locations (Availability Zones) and what the pillar says about databases in a Multi-AZ design.
demand.note: behavior: REL10-BP01 names RDS only in the multi-Region data replication sentence; no RDS-specific Multi-AZ sentence on that page.

demand.question: The official sample pattern: new subnets in another Availability Zone plus an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB plus RDS Multi-AZ. Which RDS fact makes the Multi-AZ option correct and the read replica option wrong when the stem says 'highly available' or 'without downtime'?

What a read replica is: a read-only copy fed by the engine's native asynchronous replication, with its own endpoint. Which engines support read replicas (MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2)?

How many read replicas per source DB instance: up to 15 for MariaDB, MySQL and PostgreSQL; Oracle up to 15 but 5 recommended; SQL Server lag above 5. Take the rows from the quotas page and the per-engine pages.
Automated backups must be enabled on the source (backup retention period greater than 0) before a read replica can be created. Why (the replica is created from a snapshot and catches up from logs).

Cross-Region read replicas: which engines, what they are for (disaster recovery, reads close to users, migration between Regions), that replication is asynchronous and lags, and that an encrypted source needs a KMS key in the destination Region.

Promoting a read replica: it becomes a standalone, writable DB instance; replication stops; it keeps its data; used for disaster recovery, for sharding, and for a migration cutover. Can a promotion be undone?

Can a read replica be Multi-AZ itself; can the source be Multi-AZ; what happens to replicas when the source fails over; cascading read replicas (a replica of a replica) and the chain limits per engine.
Replica lag: the ReplicaLag metric, common causes (write-heavy source, undersized replica), and the recommendation to size the replica like the source.

Multi-AZ versus read replica (the pair FREQUENCY section 3 says decides questions): synchronous versus asynchronous, one endpoint versus a separate endpoint, no reads from the standby versus read scaling, same Region versus also cross-Region, availability versus performance. Each cell needs a fact.

When to use read replicas: read-heavy workloads, reporting and analytics queries that would slow the primary, serving reads in another Region, and as a DR copy. When they are the wrong answer (write scaling, 'no downtime' for the primary).
A read replica is read-only: can writes be sent to it; can it have a different instance class or storage than the source; can it be stopped?
Read replicas of a Multi-AZ DB cluster and a DB instance read replica from a Multi-AZ DB cluster: what exists and what the limits are.
Delayed replication: RDS for MySQL supports a replication delay; RDS for PostgreSQL added delayed read replicas on 2025-08-22. Use: recover from an accidental DROP TABLE without a full restore.
Read replica cost: billed as a standard DB instance at the same rates; cross-Region replication also pays data transfer. When does the bill start and end (FAQ)?
Replication from an external (on-premises or EC2) MySQL or PostgreSQL to RDS, and from RDS outward (export replication): what the guide says exists, in one sentence each, as a pointer only.
demand.note: register-26: fetched MySQL.Procedural.Importing.External.Repl; binary log file replication with a MySQL or MariaDB instance outside RDS

demand.question: What Amazon RDS Proxy is: a fully managed, highly available database proxy that pools and shares database connections, in one sentence from the guide and one from the product page.
Which engines RDS Proxy supports: RDS for MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server, and Aurora MySQL and Aurora PostgreSQL. Which versions, from the feature page?

When to use RDS Proxy: serverless and Lambda functions that open many short connections, 'too many connections' errors, unpredictable bursts, applications that hold idle connections. The stem signals.

How RDS Proxy improves failover: it keeps application connections open and routes to the new primary, so failover is faster and the application does not need to re-resolve DNS. Any number AWS states (the product page: reduces failover time by up to 66 percent?) must be quoted verbatim.

Connection pooling and multiplexing: a pool of connections to the database, application connections share them, and the proxy enforces limits (MaxConnectionsPercent, MaxIdleConnectionsPercent, connection borrow timeout).
Session pinning: what causes a connection to be pinned to one client (session variables, prepared statements, certain SQL), and why pinning removes the benefit of multiplexing.

Authentication through the proxy: database credentials live in AWS Secrets Manager; clients can use IAM authentication to the proxy; end-to-end IAM authentication (added 2025-09-12); TLS between client and proxy.

Network placement: the proxy lives in your VPC, is reachable only through private IP addresses in the VPC (not from the public internet), and needs security groups and subnets in at least two Availability Zones.
Proxy endpoints: the default endpoint, additional endpoints, read-only endpoints (Aurora clusters only?), and cross-VPC endpoints. Which exist for RDS DB instances versus Aurora?

RDS Proxy pricing: charged per vCPU per hour of the underlying DB instance, with a minimum per proxy (hypothesis: two vCPUs), no charge for the proxy's own data transfer. Take the dimensions from the pricing page.
When RDS Proxy is not worth its cost: few long-lived connections, workloads that pin every session, a single EC2 application with a client-side pool. The 'but not if' column.
demand.note: behavior: No AWS sentence says when the proxy is 'not worth its cost' for few long-lived connections or an app with its own pool; the FAQ 'connect directly' answer is with the FAQ lens (rds-proxy-faq-adds-5-ms-connect-directly).

demand.question: Lambda to RDS without a proxy: why many concurrent function invocations exhaust max_connections, and the console 'connect a Lambda function' setup that creates the proxy and the networking.
demand.note: behavior: No sentence found stating that many concurrent Lambda invocations exhaust max_connections; looked in lambda-rds-connect, rds-proxy-planning, www/rds/faqs.

demand.question: RDS Proxy with Multi-AZ DB clusters and with Blue/Green Deployments: supported since 2023-11-09; what the proxy does during a switchover.

RDS Proxy limitations: engines and versions, no support for some features (for example cross-Region, some authentication plugins), one proxy per database instance limit?, quotas on proxies per account.
Connections without a proxy: max_connections depends on the instance class memory (the DBInstanceClassMemory formula), the DatabaseConnections metric, and 'too many connections' as a symptom.
demand.note: behavior: DBInstanceClassMemory formula not mined (USER_ParamValuesRef/CHAP_Limits are numbers-lens pages).

demand.question: Automated backups: a daily full snapshot plus transaction logs; backup retention period 0 to 35 days; what the default retention is (console versus CLI); 0 disables automated backups.
The backup window: a daily period you choose or RDS assigns; what happens if a backup needs longer than the window; I/O suspension on Single-AZ during the snapshot.

Point-in-time recovery: restore to any second inside the retention period up to the latest restorable time (typically within the last five minutes), and the restore always creates a new DB instance with a new endpoint.
Manual DB snapshots: user-initiated, kept until you delete them, survive deletion of the instance; the quota of manual snapshots per Region (hypothesis 100).

Deleting a DB instance: the final snapshot option, that automated backups are deleted with the instance unless 'retain automated backups' is chosen (kept for the retention period), and that manual snapshots stay.

Copying a snapshot: to another Region, to another account (cross-Region and cross-account copy in one step since 2025-09-23), copying an unencrypted snapshot into an encrypted one, and the KMS key requirement in the destination Region.

Sharing a snapshot: only manual snapshots can be shared (automated backups must be copied first); a snapshot encrypted with the AWS managed key cannot be shared; sharing an encrypted snapshot needs a customer managed key shared through its key policy; public sharing only for unencrypted snapshots.

Cross-Region automated backups (backup replication): which engines support it, that the replicated backups allow point-in-time recovery in the destination Region, the separate retention period in the destination, and the KMS key for encrypted sources.
Exporting snapshot data to Amazon S3: Apache Parquet, no impact on the DB instance, queried with Athena or Redshift Spectrum, which engines, and that the export is of a snapshot, not a live instance.
AWS Backup with RDS: centralized backup plans, cross-account and cross-Region copy, continuous backups for point-in-time recovery, Vault Lock; the pointer to chapter 24.
demand.note: behavior: Continuous backup/PITR, Vault Lock, cross-account copy are in the AWS Backup guide (chapter 24).

demand.question: Restoring from a snapshot: a new DB instance with a new endpoint; the default parameter group and security group apply unless specified; you can change instance class, storage type, and Multi-AZ at restore; the application must be repointed.

How to keep backups longer than 35 days (retention policy design): manual snapshots, copying automated backups to manual, AWS Backup plans with longer retention, snapshot export. Which is the 'least operational overhead' answer?
Backup storage billing: backup storage up to the size of provisioned storage is free per Region; beyond that, charged per GB-month; snapshots kept after deleting an instance are charged.

Blue/Green Deployments: a green staging copy kept in sync by logical replication, switchover with guardrails, typical switchover time (guide: under one minute; What's New 2026-01-20: under five seconds), engines (MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL), uses (major version upgrade, schema change, storage change since 2024-11-20).

Stopping a DB instance: stopped for up to seven days, then RDS starts it automatically; while stopped you pay for storage and backups, not instance hours; which deployments cannot be stopped (Multi-AZ SQL Server, instances with read replicas, read replicas).

Backup and retention policy design: snapshot frequency (automated daily plus logs, manual for milestones, AWS Backup for schedules such as hourly), RPO given by PITR, and what 'retain for seven years' implies.
Encryption at rest with AWS KMS: what it covers (the instance's storage, automated backups, read replicas, snapshots, logs), and that it can be turned on only when the instance is created.

Encrypting an existing unencrypted DB instance: snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption, restore the copy, repoint the application. Can encryption be turned off later? Can an encrypted instance have an unencrypted replica?

Encryption limitations: the KMS key must be in the same Region; a cross-Region replica or snapshot copy needs a key in the destination Region; an encrypted read replica must use the same key as the source in the same Region; the AWS managed key aws/rds versus a customer managed key.
Encryption in transit: TLS with the RDS certificate bundle; forcing TLS (rds.force_ssl for PostgreSQL, require_secure_transport for MySQL); certificate authority rotation.
Transparent Data Encryption (Oracle, SQL Server) versus RDS encryption at rest: engine-native versus KMS at the storage layer. One sentence each.

IAM database authentication: a token instead of a password, token lifetime (hypothesis 15 minutes), which engines, the connection rate guidance (changed 2026-06-30: connection rate scaling), and when the exam prefers it (no stored passwords, temporary credentials).
demand.note: numbers: Connection rate guidance: the current UsingWithRDS.IAMDBAuth page states no connections-per-second number (the 'Recommendations' section anchor is named ConnectionsPerSecond but holds only token size and temporary credential advice). Change item 2026-06-30 'Connection Rate Scaling' is for the decisions lens.

demand.question: Secrets Manager integration: RDS manages the master user password in Secrets Manager with automatic rotation (default rotation interval, hypothesis seven days); the answer to 'rotate database credentials without code changes'.
Network security: a DB subnet group needs subnets in at least two Availability Zones; security groups control access; the 'publicly accessible' setting; the private subnet default of the book's labs.
Security best practices from the guide: least-privilege IAM, security groups, encryption, no public access, audit logs to CloudWatch Logs, database activity streams (pointer only).

Parameter groups versus option groups: parameters configure the engine (static ones need a reboot, dynamic ones apply at once), options add engine features; a custom parameter group is needed to change any parameter.
The maintenance window: when RDS applies pending changes and patches, that some changes cause an outage, and how 'apply immediately' interacts with it.
RDS event notification: event categories (failover, backup, maintenance), delivery through SNS, and EventBridge rules on RDS events.

The pricing dimensions of Amazon RDS: DB instance hours by class and engine (on-demand or reserved), storage per GB-month by type, provisioned IOPS and throughput, backup storage, snapshot export, data transfer, Extended Support, and the Multi-AZ multiplier. Which ones appear in cost questions?

demand.question: Reserved DB instances: one-year or three-year terms, payment options (all, partial, no upfront), that a Multi-AZ reservation covers both instances, size flexibility within a family for some engines, and cancellation rules.

Hypothesis (FRESHNESS): Database Savings Plans (announced 2025-12) cover Amazon RDS. Does the RDS FAQ or pricing page say so, and what discount does it state? Older questions only know reserved instances.
How a Multi-AZ deployment is billed (the standby is a second instance at the Multi-AZ rate), how a stopped instance is billed, and how a read replica is billed (FAQ Billing section).
The AWS Free Tier for Amazon RDS as the FAQ states it today (changed 2025-07-15 for new accounts to a credit model): what to tell a reader who sees '750 hours' in an older question.

RDS versus Aurora: engines Aurora does not offer (Oracle, SQL Server, Db2, MariaDB), replica count and storage model as the reason to move, and when RDS is the right answer ('needs Oracle', 'minimal change', 'smallest cost for a small database'). Well-Architected performance efficiency: use purpose-built data stores; what the page says about relational databases and when to pick another store.

Disaster recovery options with RDS and their trade-offs: cross-Region read replica (promote in a disaster), cross-Region automated backups (PITR in the other Region), periodic snapshot copy, and AWS Backup copy. Which gives the lowest RPO and RTO and which is the cheapest?
